1:
Robertson notes that the verb Paul uses is the regular word for letters of commendation, and that this verse and the next together constitute the whole recommendation; her name means bright or radiant. Barnes and Ellicott both infer from the earnestness with which the Romans are told to receive her that she carried the letter herself, or at least travelled with those who did, which fixes the place of writing at Corinth; Gill takes the same view from the subscription. Barnes observes further that the names through the chapter are chiefly Greek, belonging to people who had removed from Greece to Rome for commerce, and he presses one absence hard: the name of Peter does not occur in the catalogue, which he calls conclusive evidence against the Papists that Peter was not then known by Paul to be in Rome. Cenchrea, all agree, was the eastern of Corinth's two harbours, nine miles from the city, opening on the Aegean as Lechaeum opened on the Ionian sea. Gill and Henry take "our sister" as a relation not natural but spiritual, Henry adding that Christ and his apostles had some of their best friends among devout women.

Whether the word rendered servant is here a title of office is the chief question, and the commentators divide. Ellicott would keep the technical term and translate deaconess, calling this the first mention of women-deacons, whose necessity would make itself felt wherever women were kept in the stricter seclusion usual in Greece and parts of the East; Robertson agrees, and rests the technical sense chiefly on the addition of the words "of the church," which he thinks turns a general description into a designation. Wesley states it flatly, that in the apostolic age grave and pious women were appointed deaconesses in every church, and Clarke and Barnes both write as though the order were beyond dispute. Calvin dissents. The word, he says, does not necessarily prove the point, being used often of anyone who does service and contributes help to others; he grants that Origen and Chrysostom read it of an office, and that an order of the kind did arise, but insists that this belongs to the times after the apostles, so that there is no reason to believe Phebe belonged to it. What she was, on his account, was a woman of wealth and influence, carrying on some business that took her to Rome, and a great helper of the cause and of Paul himself.

On what such women did there is no quarrel. Clarke describes them attending female converts at baptism, instructing the catechumens, visiting the sick and those in prison, and performing whatever offices for the female part of the church could not with propriety be performed by men; they were chosen from the most experienced, ordinarily widows who had borne children, and were ordained by imposition of the bishop's hands. Barnes gives the same reason, the seclusion of women among the Gentiles, and cites the Apostolical Constitutions for the direction to ordain a deaconess faithful and holy for the ministries toward the women, and Pliny's letter to Trajan for the two maid-servants called ministrae whom he put to the torture. But Barnes and Henry are equally firm on the limit: they were never regarded as an order of ministers, and were not suffered to preach to congregations; the service was one of charity and hospitality, and Henry guesses the church met at Phebe's house. Clarke traces the order's extinction in the Latin Church by the eleventh century and its survival among the Greeks until the twelfth; Calvin ends less kindly, holding that this most sacred function, when the state of things had grown worse, degenerated into the idle order of nuns, and has so fallen away from its beginning that between some sanctuaries of chastity and a common brothel there is no difference at all.
2:
The request is modest — Gill takes it as asking that they receive her into their houses and their hearts, and admit her to church fellowship as one belonging to the Lord — but the title Paul gives her is not. Barnes explains that the word rendered succourer properly means a patron or protector, applied by the Greeks to one who took up the cause of others, and especially to one who managed the cause of strangers before the courts; an honourable appellation, which applied to Phebe will mean that she had received Christians into her house and ministered to the sick. Robertson notes that the feminine form is old and rare, occurring only here in the New Testament and not at all in the papyri, and that Paul's word for assisting her is the very one he uses of the help the Lord gave him at his trial. Ellicott makes the succour an exercise of her office as deaconess, and guesses that Paul's own share in it came during an illness; Clarke supposes she was known for entertaining the preachers who came to Cenchrea. Theodoret draws a lesson from the place: Cenchrea being only a large village of Corinth, we may admire a gospel which in so short a time had filled not the towns only but the villages, and raised there a church great enough to have a woman serving as deaconess; she received Paul into one house for a short time, and he has opened the whole world to her.

Prisca — the reading Clarke and Ellicott both prefer to the diminutive Priscilla — is named before her husband, and what to make of that divides the commentators. Robertson observes that this order holds everywhere save in two places, which he thinks shows her the more prominent, and suggests she may have been a noble Roman lady married to a Jew of Pontus who worked at tents; Ellicott calls the precedence remarkable and infers that she was the more active and conspicuous. Calvin reads it as honour done deliberately, and turns it back on the apostle: the modesty of the holy man shines out here, for he disdained not to have a woman as his associate in the work of the Lord, nor was he ashamed to confess it. Gill will have none of it. Her being named first, he says, is without design, and he appeals to the rabbinic rule that there is neither first nor last in the Scriptures, strict order being often inverted with nothing depending on it; the reasons commonly assigned, that she was converted first or had more zeal, he dismisses as uncertain and impertinent.

What the couple did for Paul is vividly said and never explained. Barnes and Gill both take the phrase from the block and the axe, the neck bowed to the executioner's sword, and both treat it as figurative for hazarding their lives; Robertson notes that the verb is used in this sense only here. As to the occasion, Clarke and Ellicott confess they can do no more than guess, Ellicott inclining to the tumult at Ephesus, Robertson to the uproar raised by Demetrius, and Gill and Calvin to the insurrection at Corinth when Paul was dragged before Gallio. Barnes and Wesley both press why the Gentile churches join in the thanks: they owed their founder to the couple's courage, and Calvin adds that the life of such a man was an incomparable treasure. Calvin lingers over the house that follows: Paul could not have more splendidly adorned their household than by giving it the title of a church. Some of the Fathers, he notes, took the meaning to be that the family, being all religious, was itself the church; he rejects this as inconsistent with the state of things at the time, when believers had no temples to meet in and private houses were their churches.
5:
Chrysostom defends the passage against its readers: many who seem extremely good men hasten over this part of the epistle as superfluous, because it is a catalogue of names — yet goldsmiths are careful even of the little fragments, while these pass over great cakes of gold, and it is possible even from bare names to find a great treasure. Clarke insists on the plain sense: in these primitive times no such places existed as those we now call churches, the word signifying the congregation and not the building. Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson say the same, adding that the Roman Christians probably had several such houses. Theodoret takes it as evidence of their piety, that they instructed their household in virtue and performed the sacred rites within their walls. Wesley draws a sharper conclusion: as yet the Christians at Rome had neither bishops nor deacons, so far were they from any shadow of papal power, and there seems to have been in the whole city but this one domestic church. Whether Epenetus was firstfruits of Achaia or Asia is a question of text. Clarke reports that Asia is the reading of the chief manuscripts and that Griesbach admitted it; Ellicott says we ought certainly to read Asia, the parallel in the Corinthian letter having corrupted this one, and Calvin agrees the copies favour it. If Achaia stands, Clarke and Calvin suggest he may have belonged to the household of Stephanas, there called the firstfruits. Calvin adds that whoever is first called in time has a prerogative of honour — but keeps it only when the end answers to the beginning.

Mary's labour is praised without our being told what it was, and even its objects are uncertain. Gill notes that many copies read that she laboured on you rather than us, and thinks the saints at Rome the likelier objects; Ellicott takes the shorter way, that the readers knew what Paul meant and it is useless to conjecture. Clarke lets the obscurity stand as its own commendation: her works, hidden from men, are with God, and her name recorded with honour in the book of life. At the next names difficulties multiply. Gill holds that Junia should be read Junias and thinks the pair both men, against Grotius's guess that they were husband and wife; Robertson says the name may be masculine or feminine, and Clarke, thinking Junia a woman, would render the next word relatives rather than kinsmen. Barnes alone takes that word of actual relatives.

Whether Andronicus and Junia were apostles is the chapter's sharpest division. Barnes argues at length that they were not, urging that there is no account of their appointment, that Paul would have written distinguished apostles had he meant it, and that the office existed to bear witness to the resurrection, which they are nowhere said to have done; all the phrase implies is that they were known to the apostles and honoured by them. Calvin disagrees, holding that the words can hardly admit any other meaning than that they were apostles — not of the first order established in the twelve, but in the wider use by which Barnabas is so called, of those who planted churches by carrying the doctrine of salvation from place to place. Theodoret is more emphatic still: they are of note not among the disciples but among the teachers, and not among ordinary teachers but among the Apostles; Robertson thinks this the natural sense. Ellicott holds the balance: the phrase judged by itself would more naturally mean distinguished as apostles, and the title was not confined to the twelve, since James the Lord's brother and Barnabas both bear it — yet on the whole he thinks it best to render, highly esteemed by the apostolic circle. All agree the two were in Christ before Paul, and Theodoret ends by admiring the humble-mindedness of the apostle in saying so.
8:
Almost nothing is known of these men beyond their names, and the commentators fall back on what the names show. Ellicott and Robertson note that Amplias is a contracted form of Ampliatus, which the oldest manuscripts read, and that the name recurs in connection with the imperial household; so does Urbanus, a common slave name meaning city-bred, and Stachys, a Greek word for an ear of grain which Ellicott finds in the inscriptions as a court physician's name. Gill adds that Urbanus has since been taken by many popes — few of whom, he remarks, have deserved the character given here of a helper in Christ. What they press is that the affection is not natural but spiritual. Gill observes that Paul loved Amplias not for kindred or riches but for the Lord's sake; Theodoret makes the point more compactly, that to be called beloved in the Lord is no slight praise but a demonstration of a man's excellences, and that Urbanus is honoured higher still, as a helper in the preaching and in the sufferings for Christ's sake.

Apelles is commended as approved, and here the sense is agreed. Robertson glosses it the tried and true, Barnes as one approved and beloved by Christ, Ellicott as one whose fidelity has been tested and has stood, Clarke as a man who had given the highest proofs of the depth of his religion; Theodoret calls it a testimony of the highest virtue, since to have no alloy of dross is the summit of excellences. Gill reports that Origen doubted whether this was not Apollos, and answers that had it been so Paul would surely have said more of so eminent a preacher, besides that Apollos did not live at Rome. Over the name's nationality Gill and Ellicott part company. Ellicott takes Horace's well-known phrase, let the Jew Apella believe it, as using a typical Jewish name; Gill insists Horace means not a circumcised Jew in general, as many have thought, but a particular person of that name — adding that it matters little whether the man here was Jew or Gentile.

The last two salutations are addressed not to men but to households, and the commentators think they know which. Ellicott identifies Aristobulus as a grandson of Herod the Great who lived privately at Rome on friendly terms with Claudius, so that his household may have passed to the emperor by bequest, and Narcissus as the famous freedman of Claudius, put to death a few years before this letter, whose household would have passed by confiscation while keeping his name; he concedes the identification falls short of certain, and Robertson reports Lightfoot to the same effect. Clarke agrees that both were probably dead, which is why only their households are greeted, and that Aristobulus may have been an unconverted Roman of distinction with Christians among his slaves; but on Narcissus he demurs, seeing no reason to suppose the freedman named by Suetonius and Tacitus is the person Paul designed. Calvin takes the identification and makes it preach: Narcissus was notorious for many crimes, and the more wonderful was the goodness of God which penetrated that impure house — not that Narcissus himself was converted, but that a house which was like hell should be visited by the grace of Christ, so that servants need not wait for their masters, but every one ought to follow Christ for himself. Clarke, Wesley and Theodoret all read the added clause, those who are in the Lord, as showing the families divided and the faithful only a few. Calvin closes with two observations: that no splendid titles appear here, all whom Paul names being the obscure and ignoble at Rome, and that it would have been unbecoming to pass Peter by in so long a catalogue — as Paul must have done, if we believe the Romanists that he was then at Rome.
12:
Tryphena and Tryphosa are taken by Robertson and Wesley for sisters, possibly twins, both names coming from the verb to live luxuriously. What their labour was is disputed. Gill denies flatly that it can mean labouring in the word or in the public ministry of it, since the apostle forbade that and would not then commend them for it; he makes it their usefulness with their purses, in relieving the poor and supplying the ministers. Barnes takes a middle course, that they performed the office of deaconesses or ministered to the sick, and by example and perhaps instruction laboured to spread Christianity in their proper sphere. Clarke will have none of this. We learn from the verse, he says, that Christian women as well as men laboured in the ministry of the word, and many have spent much useless labour in endeavouring to prove that these women did not preach: a woman might prophesy if her head were covered, and whoever prophesied spoke to edification, exhortation and comfort — than which no preacher can do more. If women thus prophesied, then women preached. He does add a limit: there is much more implied in the Christian ministry, of which men only, and men called of God, are capable. Theodoret keeps to the general, that the labour was one of hospitality or fasting or some such virtue, and that Persis has the ampler praise for the ampler zeal; Robertson notes she is not Paul's beloved but the beloved of the whole church.

Over Rufus the question is what chosen means. Barnes reads election, rendering elect in the Lord; Robertson answers, not the elect but the select. Clarke argues from usage that the word often means choice or excellent, citing the chosen men of Israel and choice gifts; Gill and Ellicott arrive at the same sense, an eminent Christian of the highest form. Theodoret keeps both senses at once, calling it a most enviable encomium because many are called but few chosen. Several think they can name the man: Gill, Ellicott and Wesley recall that Mark's Gospel describes Simon of Cyrene as the father of Alexander and Rufus, and Ellicott adds that since tradition holds this Gospel was written at Rome, the same Rufus may be meant. On the mother they are unanimous and warm. Clarke denies she was Paul's own mother, and explains that among the ancients whoever acted a kind and instructing part to another was styled father or mother of that person, quoting Terence: thou art his father by nature, I by instruction. Barnes calls it an instance of Paul's delicacy; Theodoret puts it best, that nature made her the mother of Rufus, but respect for her virtue made her the mother of Paul.

The last cluster of names yields little but itself. Ellicott observes that Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes and the names following all occur in inscriptions relating to the imperial household, and that without identifying individuals, which would be precarious, one may note the coincidence with the mention of Caesar's household in the letter to Philippi. Robertson says of Hermas simply that he is not the author of the Shepherd. Gill reports the contrary tradition, that Hermas was brother of Pope Pius the First and author of the Shepherd, but grants that all of it is uncertain; Clarke, who thinks the identification probable, still lays down the sounder rule, that it is in vain to look for identity of persons in similarity of names. Robertson and Theodoret take the brethren who are with them for another company of the faithful, perhaps a little church meeting in someone's house. Wesley draws the pastoral point: it could not but encourage the poor to be saluted by name, who perhaps did not know the apostle had heard of them, and while he forgets none who are worthy, he adjusts his salutation to the degrees of worth.
15:
Robertson finds the last names as servile as the rest: Philologus another common slave name, Julia the commonest name for female slaves in the imperial household. He notices what is missing — the sister of Nereus is greeted but not named — and makes the unnamed saints who are with them a point of their own: these, the and others, constitute the great majority in all our churches. Clarke says of the whole group that nothing certain is known, some names being so ambiguous that we cannot tell whether they belonged to men or women. What Clarke presses, at more length than anything else here, is who is not saluted. Peter, on the Roman reckoning, must have been at Rome; but had he been, Paul would have greeted him first, and would not have named Andronicus and Junia as of note among the apostles while passing the head of the church over in silence. It is a loss of time, Clarke concludes, to refute such groundless pretensions, and very likely Peter never saw the city. Wesley makes the argument in a sentence: no one in this catalogue was of an eminence comparable to Peter's, so his absence means the whole Roman tradition of episcopal succession fails in its most fundamental article.

The holy kiss was a real custom, which the commentators describe rather than allegorise. Barnes calls it a salutation practised at all times and particularly in the East, and takes the word holy as guarding against improper familiarity. Robertson makes it the near-eastern equivalent of the western handshake; Wesley says the ancient Christians closed all their solemn offices with it, men saluting men and women women. Clarke adds the reason it ended, which was not abuse but numbers — the church growing so large the thing became impossible, and the shaking of hands now substituted. Ellicott catches a point the others pass over: Paul does not send this greeting himself but tells those assembled at the reading to greet each other, so that it is their own act; Theodoret says the same, that being absent he salutes them through one another. Gill alone doubts that any outward action is meant. He treats the phrase as an allusion only, and holds that Paul intends sincere goodwill rather than a rite; the word holy distinguishes it both from an unchaste kiss and from a hypocritical one, such as Joab gave Amasa while stabbing him, or Judas when he cried hail master.

Calvin gathers the history and then draws the sting. He cites a homily of Chrysostom showing that Christians kissed before partaking of the Supper and then bestowed their alms, and Grotius explains the point of it: among the orientals men kissed the mouth only of their equals and gave their hands to inferiors, so that the kiss declared all in the church equal. But it arose from local habit, Calvin says, and binds all nations no more than the washing of feet; Paul's object was not to enjoin a ceremony but to regulate a practice already in use. From the ancient rite, he adds, has come the practice of the Papists in kissing the paten and bestowing an offering — the first mere superstition, the second serving no purpose but to satisfy the avarice of the priests, if that can be satisfied. On the greeting that closes the verse, Clarke and Ellicott agree that the word all belongs in the text, Griesbach having received it on the best manuscripts, and both take Paul to speak for the churches of his founding through Greece and Asia. Calvin prefers the narrower view that Corinth is meant, thinking it improbable Paul should send greetings on the mere assumption that every church he had planted wished Rome well. Theodoret is content with the grandeur of it: from the whole world, so to speak, he salutes the Empress of the world.
17:
The warning breaks in among the greetings. Gill supposes Paul placed it here on purpose, that it might be the more noticed; Henry sees a logic in the order, that having laboured to unite them by endearing salutations, it was not improper to subjoin a caution against those whose principles were destructive of Christian love. Barnes makes it the letter's whole burden returning — peace between Jewish and Gentile converts pressed so upon him that even after the epistle is apparently finished he takes it up again. Chrysostom is struck by the manner: Paul exhorts not as a counsellor but as a servant, calling them brethren and supplicating them. On the word rendered mark all agree it means sustained attention. Robertson glosses it as keeping an eye on something so as to avoid it, Chrysostom as searching such men out thoroughly, and Clarke reports manuscripts reading look sharply after them. Wesley infers plainly that there were such men at Rome also. Henry presses hardest, because the pretences are plausible when the projects are pernicious: do not look only at the divisions and offences, but run up those streams to the fountain. A danger discovered, he says, is half prevented.

What the two evils are, and how they stand to each other, is less agreed. Robertson gives the first its literal force, standings apart, and Ellicott the second as setting traps for the unwary. Barnes separates them sharply: the one means parties and factions, the other such a course of life as leads others into sin — the Jew forming a party on the pretence of superior holiness, the bold Gentile convert deriding the Jew's scruples and so leading him to sin against conscience. Calvin orders them the other way: Paul names first the effect, divisions, then the cause, offences, for the Gentile Christians by their eating gave offence to the believing Jews, and that offence led to the separation — the quarrel over meats and days handled earlier in the letter. On who the men were there is little disagreement. Henry names the judaizing teachers who under the Christian name kept up the Mosaic ceremonies; Barnes and Theodoret say the same, Theodoret noting that the phrase contrary to the doctrine which you have learned is that of a man who admires the teaching they already had. Chrysostom traces the sequence furthest back: division is the devil's weapon and the subversion of the church, for while the body is joined in one he has no power to enter; division comes of opinions contrary to the apostles, and such opinions of slavery to the belly.

How far the avoiding goes divides them again. Clarke takes it strictly — give such men no countenance and no fellowship, and let them have neither kiss of charity nor of peace; Henry is as strict, bidding them shun all communion, since such men's word will eat as does a canker. Barnes narrows it: they were to be avoided as teachers, and the command means no harsh treatment, but that the faithful disregard whatever they said that tended to alienation; Wesley reduces it to avoiding all unnecessary intercourse. Calvin, sternest of them on the men themselves, is the most careful about the principle. It is impious, he grants, to divide those who agree in the truth of Christ; but it is shameful sophistry to defend, under pretext of peace and unity, a union in lies and impious doctrines. The Papists have no ground to seek countenance here against the Reformers, for what they impugn is not the gospel of Christ but the falsehoods by which it has been obscured; Paul condemns not all discords but those which destroy agreement in the orthodox faith. The proof lies in the clause about the doctrine they had learned — for it was the duty of the Romans themselves, before they were taught, to depart from the habits of their fathers.
18:
The mark of false teachers is a motive. Gill says they preach themselves and not Christ, seeking worldly honour and wealth, and bringing meats and drinks into a kingdom that does not consist of them; Barnes generalises it, that the authors of parties in church and state alike act for the indulgence of some earthly appetite, to obtain office or property or dominion. Clarke is fiercest: such men intrude into the church to get a secular support, and feed themselves and not the flock — and when asked whom he means, he answers that he means no soul and no party but such as the description suits, and that whoever is angry has found the cap fits. Theodoret alone names the party, holding it plain from the belly that Paul speaks of the Jews, whose gluttony he perpetually condemns. Ellicott alone hesitates: the phrase recalls those who made a god of their belly in the letter to Philippi, but it is not quite clear the same class is meant, selfish indulgence being a common goal to which many diverse errors lead.

On the method there is more agreement and finer detail. Wesley divides the two phrases neatly: the good words concern themselves, in great promises, the fair speeches concern you, in praise and flattery; Robertson notes the first compound occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Barnes traces the procedure as an art drawn with a master's hand — first smooth pretences of a love of truth, then an artful mingling of attentions and flatteries — and remarks that it would have been happy had it been confined to Paul's own times. Calvin marks the difference from honest ministry: the preachers of the gospel have their courtesy too, but joined with honesty, so that they neither soothe men with vain praises nor flatter their vices, whereas impostors indulge men's vices to keep them attached. Cyril widens it into a rule, that godliness consists of pious doctrines and virtuous practice, neither acceptable without the other — for what profit is it to know the doctrines and be a vile fornicator, or to be nobly temperate and an impious blasphemer? He then sorts the deceivers: the Greeks draw men away by a smooth tongue, since honey drops from a harlot's lips; those of the circumcision by misinterpreting the Scriptures; and the heretics disguise the poisoned arrows of their doctrines with the name of Christ, as though with honey.

The praise that follows is also a warning, and most see the double edge. Barnes says the obedient disposition for which the Romans were famous was just the temper to be imposed upon; Gill adds that their known readiness to believe may itself have invited the false teachers, and that having been famous for obedience they would be as notorious for disobedience if they now deserted the doctrine. Ellicott reassures before he cautions — no harm is done as yet, still it is well to be on your guard — and then catches what the others miss, that the word rendered simple here is not the word so rendered above. The first is the freedom from dishonest motives that makes a man an easy prey, a matter of natural bent; the second is the settled condition of one who has met evil and remained uncontaminated, the word meaning unmixed and pure — a sense Robertson confirms from its derivation. Calvin turns the clause against an abuse: we see here what the simplicity commended in Christians is, so that they have no claim to it who count their stupid ignorance of the word of God a high virtue; Paul approves the Romans as teachable, yet would have them exercise wisdom, lest their readiness to believe expose them to imposition. Clarke and Wesley reduce it to a rule — as knowing as possible in what is good, as ignorant as possible in what is evil.
20:
The title is read as deliberate. Clarke takes the God of peace to be one who neither sends nor favours such disturbers of his church's tranquillity; Wesley calls him the author and lover of peace, blessing the discretion just enjoined. Ellicott hears a man writing amid fightings without and fears within: the Romans have not yet felt the bitterness of divisions, he foresees that they will, and beyond that a time when all shall be hushed and the Great Adversary for ever overthrown. Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson agree the verb looks back to the first promise in Genesis, Robertson glossing it as to crush or trample underfoot. Who the Satan is that is trodden down is answered narrowly: Barnes makes him the author of every attempt to promote discord in the church, which is why those who produce divisions are called his ministers, and Clarke reports that several critics take the name as a collective term for all opposers, especially the false teachers just described.

Whether the sentence promises or prays is the question here, and they divide over the mood of one verb. Calvin is explicit that it is a promise rather than a prayer — Paul exhorts them to fight manfully and undertakes that they shall shortly be victorious — though he reports that most take it the other way, as a petition, the future standing after the Hebrew manner for an optative, and that the verb is found in that mood in some copies. Robertson reads it as Calvin does, a blessed promise of final victory, and Clarke as an undertaking that they shall be given dominion over the great adversary; Barnes hovers between, saying it denotes Paul's confidence that they would gain the victory over the arts of those sowing contention. Theodoret states it flatly as petition: having bidden them be on their guard, most opportunely does the apostle beseech God to confound the teacher of all snares and cast him beneath the feet of believers. On shortly there is more agreement. Calvin insists it is not only the last day that is meant, but that since Satan was then raging as with broken reins the Lord would soon subdue him; he was once conquered by Christ, yet not so as to keep him from renewing the war, and his final defeat does not appear in the middle of the contest. Ellicott refers the nearness rather to Paul's expectation of the Messiah's return, and Robertson answers in a phrase — shortly, as God counts time, and meanwhile patient loyalty from us.

The benediction raises a question of text. Ellicott judges the more correct reading to be simply that the grace of our Lord Jesus be with you, and notes that the four principal Graeco-Latin codices omit it here and place it later, where it stands in the Received text though wanting in the best manuscripts. Clarke reports the same omission in several ancient copies and supposes the scribes thought the words borrowed from the later verse, but refuses the inference: the apostle may have added a postscript, or two. That carries further than the textual point, for Clarke reads the verse as where Paul appears to have meant to conclude the epistle, all after it being appendix. On the sense of the grace there is no dispute. Barnes takes it as an earnest wish addressed to the Lord Jesus as the Prince of Peace, that the design of his coming might be accomplished in the prevalence of peace; Calvin makes it a prayer that they might enjoy all the blessings procured by Christ; Clarke ties it back to the warning, that without that gracious influence they can neither be kept from evil nor do anything good. Theodoret gives the sequence its shape: having pointed out the enemy, the apostle points out the Helper, for they who have obtained the divine grace possess what is invincible.
21:
Robertson treats the closing verses as a postscript carrying greetings from Paul's companions at Corinth, and Gill imagines the scene — the letter just concluding, his friends about him, one saying send my salutation to our friends at Rome, and then a second and a third, Timothy beginning. The title Paul gives him is noticed by several. Henry observes that Paul elsewhere calls Timothy his son, as an inferior, but here styles him work-fellow, as one equal with him; Theodoret makes the same comparison across the four names, that the first has the glory of a share in the work and the others of relationship, but the fellow-worker is far more honourable than the relation. Gill fills in the history — met with at Derbe, his father a Greek and his mother a believing Jewess, circumcised because of the Jews, afterwards the recipient of two letters in which Paul calls him his well-beloved son. Ellicott raises a question the others do not, and cannot answer it: in the other epistles written while Timothy was present he is joined with Paul in the salutation at the outset, and why his name is absent from the heading of this one we can hardly say — perhaps he was away when it was begun, or Paul thought a church wholly strange to him should be addressed in his own name alone. Wesley gives the reason without hesitating: Timothy had never been at Rome, and so is not named at the beginning, though here he stands before Paul's kinsmen.

The other three names invite identification, and they differ chiefly in how far they will go. On Lucius, Barnes notes the prophet and teacher of Cyrene named among the leaders at Antioch and says nothing more is known of him; Robertson allows only that he may be that man; Ellicott is more cautious, holding the name too common for anything to be asserted positively. Clarke breaks ranks and proposes Luke the evangelist, writer of the Acts. On Jason all look to the man at Thessalonica who received the apostles into his house, Clarke adding that he befriended them at the risk of both property and life. Ellicott ties it to the next word: it would be some slight argument for the identification if kinsmen were taken in the narrower sense, since there would then be a reason why Paul found hospitality in Jason's house. Sosipater is generally allowed to be the Sopater of Berea, Robertson taking the one name for the longer form of the other, and Clarke adding that he was a Jew by birth who accompanied Paul from Greece into Asia and probably into Judea.

Whether kinsmen means countrymen or relatives divides them as it did earlier in the chapter. Robertson takes the word in the wide sense, that they are all Paul's fellow-countrymen. Henry takes it both ways: they are so called not only more largely, as Jews, but as nearly allied to him in blood or affinity — and he infers from the number of them that Paul must have been of a good family, meeting so many of his kindred in several places. To this Henry adds the reflection that gives the verse its warmth, that it is a very great comfort to see the holiness and usefulness of our kindred. On what the salutations are for, Henry and Calvin agree. Henry thinks Paul added them to promote fellowship among distant saints, and because the subscribing of worthy names already known at Rome would the more recommend the letter. Calvin puts it that they served partly to foster union between those who were far asunder, and partly to let the Romans know that their brethren subscribed to the epistle — not that Paul had any need of the testimony of others, but because the consent of the godly is not a thing of small importance.
22:
The scribe steps forward in his own person, and the commentators explain how Paul's letters were made. Barnes says he employed an amanuensis, then signed his own name and added a salutation in his own hand, as he tells the Thessalonians was his practice in every epistle; Ellicott gives the reason twice over, as a mark of personal interest and as a precaution against forgery. Ellicott draws the consequence for the letter: the involved and broken style is often to be accounted for by this habit of dictation, followed by revision that was not very punctilious, so that we have the apostle's words as they came warm from his mind. Wesley supposes Tertius inserted his own greeting either at Paul's urging or by his permission; Theodoret makes him one thought worthy of the apostle's instruction, who received through that tongue the outpourings of the Spirit and was bidden write them down. Who he was nobody knows. Gill reports the guess that he was Silas, the Hebrew name meaning the same thing; Clarke objects that it is strange the name he is usually given in Scripture should not have been used here, and disposes of a bolder theory, that Paul wrote in Syriac and Tertius turned it into Greek — the man says he wrote the epistle, not that he translated it. He adds a doubt the others do not raise, that it is not clear whether the two following verses are the words of Tertius or of Paul.

Which Gaius this was cannot be settled. Barnes identifies him with the man Paul baptized at Corinth, so esteemed that John afterwards wrote him an epistle, and a wealthy citizen who opened his house for hospitality and worship; Ellicott counts three of the name and thinks the Corinthian likeliest, but observes the name was common, and Robertson says we do not know whether he is the man of the epistle. On host of the whole church there is more agreement. Barnes explains that a host entertains another without reward, and Robertson that the Greek means a guest friend and so, as here, a host of strangers. Clarke says he lodged the apostles and the messengers of the churches besides, so that he must have had property and much love to Christ's cause; Theodoret calls it the greatest praise, to have opened one's house to the nurselings of the faith and ministered even to the teachers of the whole world. Ellicott alone leaves room for something less literal, that Gaius may have lent his house for the church's meetings, or that Paul may be alluding with graceful hyperbole to a hospitality he was always ready to show.

Erastus is given a title the translators mistook. Barnes explains that chamberlain suggests the officer with charge of the king's lodgings and wardrobe, whereas the Greek is elsewhere rendered steward and here means the man who presided over the city's pecuniary affairs, and should have been rendered treasurer. Clarke describes the work — he received the tolls and customs and out of them paid the public expenses — and Robertson calls him one of the outstanding men of Corinth, while Theodoret notes that Paul calls him treasurer not of the church but of the city. But the identification raises a difficulty that Clarke and Ellicott both feel. The Erastus named elsewhere travelled with Paul, and Ellicott observes that the treasurership of such a city would involve a fixed residence; Clarke concludes that if the two are the same he cannot have held the office at this time, and reports that several suppose he had formerly held it and still kept the title, though Chrysostom thought he kept the employment too. Of Quartus almost nothing is said. Clarke does not know whether he was brother to Erastus or to Tertius and thinks nothing more is meant than that he was a Christian, one of the heavenly family.
25:
Robertson calls these closing verses the finest of Paul's doxologies, and Henry says the apostle breathes out his soul in praise, making that the end of his epistle which he made the end of his life. Where it belongs is disputed. Barnes reports that it stands in many manuscripts at the close of the fourteenth chapter but holds its proper place is here; Clarke says the reverse, that the most reputable manuscripts put these verses at the end of that chapter, which most critics suppose their proper place. Gill takes the instance of the power to be the establishing of God's people in the gospel, and Barnes that God only can keep Christians in the path of salvation, so it was well to bring that truth into view at the close. Why Paul calls the gospel his own Henry and Barnes explain alike: not that he was its author or only preacher, but that he gloried in it and had been defending its doctrines through this letter; Robertson adds that the phrase means not a book but Paul's message.

What the mystery is divides them more than one might expect. Henry takes it broadly, as our redemption by Jesus Christ, no vulgar thing hammered out by human wit but the product of the eternal counsel of God — a mystery the angels desire to look into and cannot fathom, yet of which so much is made plain as will bring us to heaven. Barnes takes it as the principal doctrines of the gospel, concealed especially from the Gentile world; Wesley makes it the calling of the Gentiles, which, plainly as the prophets had foretold it, was still hidden from many even of the believing Jews. Clarke, following Locke and Taylor, narrows it and denies Wesley's account: the calling of the Gentiles was declared in general terms by the prophets, and the point on which they gave no information was that they should be admitted without passing under the yoke of the Mosaic law — a thing he thinks peculiarly revealed to Paul. On the words rendered since the world began, Henry offers two constructions, either that the mystery was wrapped in silence from eternity, or that through the Old Testament it lay hid in the types of the ceremonial law; Barnes and Robertson render the Greek literally as in eternal times, meaning all past time.

That a mystery kept secret should be made manifest by the writings of the prophets is the difficulty of the passage, and they meet it in different ways. Henry answers that the event has given the best exposition to the prophecies, which being accomplished are explained: the prophets' preaching was dark in the ages when they lived, but what they left in writing reads otherwise now. Ellicott resolves it by the syntax: this mystery, through the corroboration it derives from the prophets, has by God's command been made known — a command he instances in the separating of Paul and Barnabas by the Holy Ghost, while Robertson observes that Paul conceives God to be in charge of the redemptive work and to give the orders. The title everlasting draws the finest remark of the passage. Barnes takes it of the God who is eternal and therefore unchanged, who concealed this truth but always intended it should be revealed; Wesley says a more proper epithet could not be, since a new dispensation infers no change in God, to whom all his works and every variation of them are known from eternity. Ellicott ends by noting that the closing phrase repeats the letter's opening, and that the preposition carries more stress than the English shows — made known so as to reach all nations; Wesley adds that it was not barely that they might know it, but enjoy it, and Clarke that they might receive circumcision of the heart in place of all Jewish rites.
27:
Barnes explains why wisdom is the attribute singled out: the doxology, interrupted by the parenthesis, resumes here, and wisdom is named because it had been displayed in the plan just described — in devising it, in adapting it to the renewing of the heart, and in the manner by which all the divine attributes were seen to harmonise. Clarke presses the point from the side of the mystery: he alone who is the fountain of wisdom had all this in himself, and glory is due for the wisdom that devised the plan and the goodness that sent Christ to execute it. Gill refers the title to the Father, the only wise God originally and essentially, though not excluding the Son and Spirit, the glory of the whole being ascribed to him through Christ. Wesley joins him who is able and the wise God, as Paul elsewhere styles Christ the wisdom and the power of God.

Ellicott gives his longest note to a grammatical difficulty the English version conceals by omitting two words. The Greek runs literally, to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever; and the relative, if it refers to God, as he thinks it was meant to, is ungrammatical, while if retained it leaves the opening words about him that is able without government. Broken constructions are frequent with Paul, he grants, but it is another matter in the last solemn words of an epistle. The difficulty is heightened by through Jesus Christ, which, cut off from the ascription of glory and attached to the only wise God, yields no satisfactory sense; the rendering some maintain, to God who through Christ has shown himself the alone wise, he calls very forced. His conclusion before the evidence is that the relative crept in without warrant — and he then finds one uncial omits it, precisely the oldest and best of all, the Codex Vaticanus, with two cursives. He weighs the objection: one would suspect the words were dropped for their difficulty, though the Vatican manuscript is peculiarly free from that charge, while doxologies so often begin with the relative that a copyist might fall into it. The probabilities balancing, he judges it likeliest that the relative slipped in early and the English version is substantially right — adding that there are exceptions to the rule that the more difficult reading is to be preferred, and this is perhaps one. Robertson settles it briefly: some manuscripts omit it.

The subscription is rejected by all who mention it. Barnes calls it the addition of another hand, and argues from sense as much as from manuscripts: Paul would not write to inform the Romans that his letter was sent by Phebe, whom he had just commended to their kindness. Clarke finds a positive error in it, since the Greek makes Phebe the writer of the epistle, which the verse about Tertius contradicts; the words are wanting in almost all the ancient manuscripts, the oldest having simply, To the Romans. Ellicott dates it: in its present form it hardly goes back beyond the ninth century, the earliest form, down to the sixth, being simply To the Romans. The closing Amen fares little better as text. Clarke observes that the word was seldom added by the inspired writers and is wanting here in almost all the ancient copies, but defends it in use rather than in text: pious readers would say it on finishing such a letter, expressing their conviction of its truth and their desire that its promises be fulfilled, so that the word is not merely harmless but useful. He ends with the prayer he thinks the epistle has been about — that the fulness of the Gentiles may be brought in and all Israel saved — and bids every pious reader say Amen to it; Wesley, closing on the same word, says the same.
